blogs.title: The Same‑Scope Principle: Federal Circuit Faults TTAB for Narrowing DuPont Factor Six After Broad Factor Two
blogs.description: The opinion polices internal consistency in the DuPont analysis. After the Board found Apex’s and CC Serve’s services highly similar—indeed legally identical in part—under factor two, it limited factor six’s crowding inquiry to credit‑card marks and excluded other banking/financing uses. The Federal Circuit called that a legal error, citing the rule that factor six, like factor two, looks to similar (not identical) goods. This post unpacks the court’s reliance on Olde Tyme Foods, Juice Generation, and Jack Wolfskin, and extracts a practice rule: define the overlap once and carry that scope across factors, or risk remand.

blogs.title: Counting Crowded Fields in Finance: From Nine “Aspire” Cards to Dozens of Financial “Aspire” Marks
blogs.description: This post examines the evidentiary calibration of the sixth DuPont factor. The Board credited nine third‑party “Aspire” credit‑card uses but treated 42 additional financial‑services uses as “essentially irrelevant,” concluding ASPIRE enjoyed a normal scope of protection. The Federal Circuit did not set a magic number, but it required a broader dataset consistent with the services overlap. We situate the case alongside Juice Generation and Jack Wolfskin on when third‑party use signals weakness, and assess how a larger universe of financial “Aspire” marks could diminish ASPIRE’s commercial or conceptual strength on remand.

blogs.title: Broad IDs, Broad Problems: Why “Banking and Financing Services” Sank Apex on DuPont Factor Two
blogs.description: The court affirmed the Board’s factor‑two finding that Apex’s broadly worded “banking and financing services” are highly similar—legally identical in part—to CC Serve’s “credit card services.” Relying on dictionary definitions and third‑party registrations, and notwithstanding CC Serve’s role as a program manager partnering with issuing banks, the Board treated credit‑card activity as squarely within the banking/finance umbrella. We parse that reasoning, note the Board’s reconstruction of “credit card services” after the ID Manual entry was deleted, and offer drafting takeaways: avoid catch‑all identifications, expressly carve out credit‑card issuance/servicing if that’s the intent, and remember that current nonuse will not rescue an overly broad ITU.

blogs.title: What Does “BANK” Buy You? Reassessing the First DuPont Factor for ASPIRE BANK After Remand
blogs.description: Because the mark‑strength assessment may change after a corrected factor‑six analysis, the Federal Circuit vacated the Board’s first‑factor ruling. This post previews the remand: how will ASPIRE compare to ASPIRE BANK in appearance, sound, connotation, and commercial impression once the mark’s strength is recalibrated? We discuss why “BANK” is typically generic/descriptive for financial services and contributes little distinctiveness, yet in a crowded field incremental differences—including added wording or design elements—can carry outsized weight. We outline plausible outcomes and the kinds of record evidence brand owners should assemble to show distinct commercial impressions.
